transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Dev Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Romero (Brightlayer Head of Platform), Priya Singh (ML Eng), Jonas Mayer (SRE)

Summary: quick scoping call to lock down benchmark plan and harness integration details — customer will provide production token traces and their client scripts; we need to decide streaming vs non-streaming baseline and define success metrics for p95/p99, throughput, and cold-start behavior. discuss security handoff and timeline.

Topics: workload sizing, harness adapter, tokenization discrepancies, streaming fallbacks, SLA/acceptance criteria, synthetic vs recorded trace runs, telemetry points to capture.

Action items (covered verbally in call above and listed again): see action_items metadata.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maria Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro — I'm Maria AE on the account, Dev is our SE, we'll run the harness work with you.
[00:12] Alex Romero: thanks, Maria. really trying to validate that we can hit our latency and cost targets before we commit to dedicated. mainly worried about long-tail token latency when we go to streaming.
[00:20] Priya Singh: yeah uh hi, Priya here. our typical request shape is fairly short-ish prompts but we do have spikes where context windows push to ~1.5k tokens. we also do lots of small chat messages streaming back to the UI.
[00:35] Dev Patel: got it. can you confirm average tokens per request and QPS during peak?
[00:40] Priya Singh: average ~120 tokens, 95th percentile payload ~800 tokens, peak QPS around 220 across the cluster.
[00:49] Jonas Mayer: and those peaks are bursty, think 30s windows where QPS jumps 3x. Also cold starts matter, we can't have long waits for the first token.
[00:58] Maria Chen: okay that's useful. Our typical benchmark matrix will include steady-state throughput, p95 and p99 token latency, cold-start tail, and resource cost per 1M tokens. For streaming specifically we'll measure token flush latency and first-byte latency.
[01:14] Alex Romero: can you explain how the harness will plug into our existing client script set? we have an internal harness with some custom auth preflight.
[01:22] Dev Patel: sure. we provide a harness adapter template in python/node that wraps your scripts. the adapter handles auth handshake and tokenization normalization — one tricky bit is different tokenizers across models, so we standardize on raw token counts from your trace then re-tokenize on the target model to drive identical token emission patterns.
[01:42] Priya Singh: re-tokenize — careful, our production uses a modified tokenizer for redaction. some tokens get masked before hitting the model. will that break the harness?
[01:51] Dev Patel: we can support pre-tokenized inputs in the adapter. if you give us the redaction rules or a pre-tokenized sample we can replay exactly. that's in scope.
[02:02] Alex Romero: what about streaming vs non-streaming cost delta — we've seen big differences with other providers when they force a non-streamed endpoint.
[02:09] Maria Chen: right, so streaming usually increases small token latency (first-byte) but reduces perceived latency for end-users and can increase CPU under certain kernels. non-streaming (batching) can improve throughput and lower cost per token but increases time-to-first-byte. We'll quantify both on your workload.
[02:28] Jonas Mayer: for acceptance criteria we want: p95 end-to-end latency < 250ms for small messages, p99 < 600ms during normal load, and under burst we want graceful degradation — e.g., fallback to a cheaper model if latency exceeds threshold.
[02:41] Dev Patel: notes — we'll run a canary playback with your 7-day token trace, then run three lab passes: 1) non-streamed batched baseline, 2) streaming optimized baseline, 3) mixed-mode with KV cache warmup. Each pass will capture token-level latencies, server CPU/GPU utilization, and network jitter.
[03:05] Priya Singh: KV cache warmup is important — our use case has a lot of repeated prefixes. how does Redwood handle prefix caching and KV cache reuse across requests?
[03:15] Dev Patel: our runtime supports prefix KV caching and can optionally pin cache entries on dedicated pools. For the harness we can simulate steady-state by pre-warming caches with a warmup script included in the harness. you'll see significant cost improvements once the KV cache is warm.
[03:31] Alex Romero: timeline? we need results before our board meeting on 2026-10-02.
[03:37] Maria Chen: if you deliver samples by 9/13, we can run baseline microbench and deliver initial results by 9/16. then schedule an extended lab for the week of 9/20 with a wrap-up report by 9/24. That meets your board date with buffer.
[03:51] Jonas Mayer: what's the expected duration of the streaming lab runs?
[03:54] Dev Patel: single full run 4-6 hours for a 7-day trace to get stable metrics; we'll parallelize with smaller 1-hour runs to get quick iterations.
[04:05] Priya Singh: A Few gotchas — our internal client scripts do asynchronous retries on 5xx which can inflate apparent QPS in a load test if not modeled correctly.
[04:16] Dev Patel: good flag. include retry logic in your scripts or annotate traces so harness suppresses retries during playback. we'll add a mode to the adapter for "no-retry replay".
[04:28] Alex Romero: security questions: SOC2, audit logs, KMS for keys — we need audit log retention and explicit KMS integration for private deployments.
[04:36] Maria Chen: we'll share SOC2 report and our security pack; for private/VPC deployments we support customer-managed KMS (HSM optional) and audit logs with configurable retention. I'll send links after the call.
[04:48] Jonas Mayer: does Redwood support per-route throttles and canary fallbacks to smaller models when capacity is constrained?
[04:54] Dev Patel: yes, smart routing supports per-route policies, canary rollouts and automatic fallback to model variants. For the POC we'll define a policy to fallback to the 8-bit quantized model if p95 breaches threshold for 2 consecutive minutes.
[05:11] Priya Singh: about telemetry — we need token-level timings, request ids, and an indicator of whether a response was served from cache. will the harness emit those?
[05:19] Dev Patel: yes, the harness will collect token emission timestamps, service-side p95/p99, resource metrics and a cache-hit flag per request. we'll publish the CSV/Prometheus and a summary dashboard.
[05:30] Alex Romero: any limitations on streaming models, like max concurrent streams per GPU?
[05:34] Dev Patel: depends on model size and compilation kernels. we'll include per-model concurrency profiles in the result set. typical numbers: for a 30B-ish model you might see fewer concurrent streams than for a smaller 7B quantized model.
[05:49] Maria Chen: let's also decide acceptance gates. I'd propose three gates: functional correctness (no errors in replay), performance gates (p95/p99 and throughput targets), and regression checks (compare Redwood previous baseline vs this run within 5% on unit cost). Agree?
[06:05] Alex Romero: sounds reasonable. explicitly: first-byte latency target for streaming < 120ms on small messages, p95 end-to-end < 250ms, cost per 1M tokens under $X (we'll fill exact $ after we see dedicated pricing).
[06:20] Priya Singh: one more — we do sensitive PHI fields that get redacted pre-tokenization. we need assurance these never leave our environment in raw form.
[06:29] Maria Chen: for the POC we can accept anonymized or redacted traces. for private deployment we can sign an NDA and offer on-prem packaging or VPC with customer-managed keys.
[06:41] Jonas Mayer: on the harness side, what about language and runtime? our platform is node-based, with a python data team.
[06:49] Dev Patel: we have both node and python adapters. recommend starting with your node scripts and using the python adapter as a reference for tokenization parity.
[06:58] Alex Romero: can we run a smoke test this week just to validate the handshake? 30 minute window is fine.
[07:02] Maria Chen: yes, if you can drop a small sample and credentials to the secure folder, Dev will run a smoke replay and share logs.
[07:10] Priya Singh: will the smoke include streaming? I'd like to validate streaming handshake and chunking.
[07:14] Dev Patel: yes we can do a short streamed replay to validate chunk boundaries and client backpressure behavior — that'll catch client-side issues early.
[07:24] Alex Romero: any thought on synthetic vs recorded trace? we want both — synthetic for stress testing and recorded for fidelity.
[07:31] Dev Patel: agreed. we'll do both: synthetic to push extremes and recorded to measure real-world costs.
[07:37] Maria Chen: quick callouts on reporting: we'll provide a detailed CSV with per-request token timing, an aggregated dashboard, and a recommendation sheet with quantization/batching knobs to hit cost targets.
[07:51] Jonas Mayer: what's the escalation path if we see a regression mid-run?
[07:54] Dev Patel: immediate rollback to previous model variant, we maintain warm standby pools for critical runs. SE on-call will triage; Maria will coordinate with your ops.
[08:03] Priya Singh: ok cool. any additional dependencies from our side? you'll need service account creds, sample traces, and confirmation on redaction rules.
[08:09] Maria Chen: correct — we'll include a checklist in the follow-up email.
[08:14] Alex Romero: last item: cost modeling — can you give a rough delta between hosted and dedicated? we prefer dedicated if the cost/unit is below a threshold but want to see hard numbers.
[08:23] Maria Chen: I'll include pricing bands for both in the follow-up; dedicated typically lowers per-token cost with higher commit but has capacity guarantees which matter for tail latency.
[08:34] Dev Patel: one nuance — quantized model variants may reduce resource usage by 2-4x depending on workload; we'll surface those tradeoffs in the recommendation sheet.
[08:45] Alex Romero: perfect. recap and next steps?
[08:48] Maria Chen: recap: Brightlayer to upload artifacts by 9/13, Redwood run baseline by 9/16, schedule lab week of 9/20, share full report by 9/24. security docs and pricing sent by 9/14. action owners in the notes.
[09:03] Priya Singh: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:05] Maria Chen: thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the lab and the smoke test.
[09:10] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional mis-hearings in technical terms (K V cache sometimes transcribed with spaces, V P C heard as V P C), filler words present. The transcript preserves spontaneous interruptions and clarifications as recorded.
